ety.text: From Middle English maught, might, miȝt, myght, from Old English maht, meaht, meht, mieht, miht, mæht (“ability, power; strength; virtue”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz (“ability, power; force, strength”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able to, to have power”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”), corresponding to Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”) + *-þiz. Equivalent to may + -th.
From Old English meahte and mihte, inflections of magan, whence English may.

senses.d: Power, strength, force, or influence held by a person or group.
ex: […]ſtrengthed with all myght, thꝛough his gloꝛious power, unto all pacience and long ſufferyng with ioifulneſſe[…]
Since every nation considers itself right, peace lies in balancing the military mights of the possible rivals.

senses.d: Physical strength or force.
ex: He pushed with all his might, but still it would not move.

senses.d: The ability to do something.
Mighty; powerful.
Possible.
Used to indicate a desired past action that was not done.
ex: You might have warned me about the thunderstorm.

senses.d: Used to indicate conditional or possible actions; would perhaps/maybe.
ex: Well, I might go to a party, but I haven't decided yet.
The characterism of an honest man: He looks not to what he might do, but what he should.

senses.d: Used concessively to admit something before making a more accurate or important statement; although
ex: I might be in a wheelchair, but I still want to be treated as a lady.
I might play football, but I do know how to read.

senses.d: Used in polite requests for permission.
ex: "Might I take the last biscuit? I wonder if I might have a little more coffee too." "Yes you may, help yourself.".

senses.d: Used to express certainty.
ex: Yeah, I think we might need something a bit sturdier.

grp.label: indicator of conditional or possible actions

Seasonal moving of animals, as mammals, birds or fish, especially between breeding and non-breeding areas.

ex: The migration of lead from a can to the food inside it can cause lead poisoning.

From Middle English mighty, mightie, mighti, myghty, miȝty, maȝty, from Old English mihtiġ, mehtiġ, meahtiġ, mæhtiġ (“mighty”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahtīg (“mighty”), from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz (“mighty”), equivalent to might + -y. Cognate with Scots michty, mychty, Saterland Frisian machtich, Dutch machtig, German Low German machtig, German mächtig, Swedish mäktig.

senses.d: A warrior of great strength and courage.
ex: And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties.

senses.d: Very strong; possessing might.
ex: He's a mighty wrestler, but you are faster than him.
Wise in heart, and mighty in strength.

senses.d: Very heavy and powerful.
ex: Thor swung his mighty hammer.
He gave the ball a mighty hit.

senses.d: Very large; hefty.
Accomplished by might; hence, extraordinary; wonderful.
ex: His mighty works
Mighty was their fuss about little matters.

senses.d: Excellent, extremely good.
ex: Tonight's a mighty opportunity to have a party.
She's a mighty cook.

senses.d: Very; to a high degree.
ex: You can leave that food in your locker for the weekend, but it's going to smell mighty bad when you come back on Monday.
Pork chops boiled with turnip greens make a mighty fine meal.
